nxdjvz: Empezar a, ponerse a, echarse a: three ways of starting
1cz98th: “Empezar a” (or “comenzar a”, more formal) + infinitive marks the start of an action, a state or a process, with no further nuance: “Empecé a trabajar en la librería en marzo”, “Empieza a hacer frío”. “Ponerse a” + infinitive shows that someone decides to start, or suddenly starts, an activity: “Llegué a casa y me puse a escribir”. It is not used with states: we don’t say “se puso a saber”.
10vqkwv: “Echarse a” is used almost only with reír, llorar, correr and temblar, for a sudden, uncontrolled start: “Cuando vio el cartel, se echó a llorar”. And if the action hasn’t started yet but is about to, you say “estar a punto de” + infinitive. Pronouns go before the conjugated verb or attached to the infinitive, never in between: “me puse a ordenarlos” or “los empecé a ordenar”.
11na12j: With “empezar”, “ponerse” and “echarse” the preposition “a” is compulsory.
qx1fm0: “Ponerse a” goes with activities; for a change of state you use “ponerse” + adjective.
1j67yu6: “Seguir” (or “continuar”) + gerund says that an action that started before has not been interrupted: “Sigo dando clases por las mañanas”. The opposite, that something you expected still hasn’t started, is said with “seguir sin” + infinitive: “Seguimos sin tener calefacción”. Careful: “seguir” changes “e” to “i” (sigo, sigues, siguió) and never goes with an infinitive: you don’t say “sigo trabajar”.
c2yck3: “Soler” + infinitive talks about what you normally do: “Suelo abrir a las cuatro”. It is only used in the present (“suelo”) and the imperfect (“solía”), and always with an infinitive. The gerund is formed with -ando (-ar) and -iendo (-er, -ir); some verbs change the vowel (durmiendo, pidiendo, diciendo) or use “y” (leyendo, oyendo, yendo).
1lvtodn: If in English you say “still + -ing”, think of “seguir + gerund”; if you say “still not”, think of “seguir sin”.
1exdoyi: “Seguir” goes with a gerund, not an infinitive.
1pz72ow: For what still isn’t happening, you say “seguir sin” + infinitive.
vwbedz: “Soler” has no preterite: in the past you use “solía”.

112ok0d: The gerund: -ando, -iendo, -yendo and the changing vowel
i5lbmt: The gerund is always stressed on the syllable “-an-” or “-ien-”: tra-ba-JAN-do, a-pren-DIEN-do. In -ir verbs that change their vowel in the present, “e” becomes “i” and “o” becomes “u”: pidiendo, sintiendo, diciendo, siguiendo, durmiendo, muriendo. That vowel can be heard clearly and it is easy to mix it up if you aren’t expecting it.
1y6phbc: When the stem ends in a vowel, the “i” of “-iendo” becomes “y”: leyendo, oyendo, cayendo, construyendo; and the gerund of “ir” is “yendo”. Pronounce that “y” as a soft consonant, just like in “haya” from week 6.

11v7xco: A profile in a local newspaper
1sfpm4h: The “People of Rosario” section of the city newspaper publishes this profile for the bookshop’s first anniversary.
ieu3xy: A year ago, on a corner in Pichincha that had been empty for some time, Paula Ferraro hung up a handwritten sign: “Second-hand books, coffee and conversation”. Nobody expected much from such a small shop. However, within a few weeks the neighbours started dropping in to have a look, and many of them stayed.
vahlk: Paula, who is a literature teacher, still works at a secondary school in the mornings. “Although I end up exhausted, I don’t want to give up teaching,” she explains. In the afternoons she usually serves alone, although on Saturdays her brother Tomás, who takes care of the book launches, helps her. The best attended was the one by a poet from the neighbourhood: when she finished reading, the audience started a standing ovation and she burst out laughing from nerves.
m9x4nl: Not everything was easy. The paperwork for the licence took four months and the shop still has no heating. “In July we gave the workshops wearing gloves,” she remembers, laughing. To stay afloat, Paula sells coffee and home-made cakes from a neighbour, and every month she organises a book-swap fair on the pavement: if you bring two books, you take one.
1vuhfl3: The project keeps growing. Paula is looking for someone who can give writing workshops for teenagers, and she wants to open on Sundays when she has someone she trusts at the till. “I’m glad the neighbourhood has made the bookshop its own,” she says. Her advice for anyone who wants to take the risk? “I’d start small and listen to people a lot.”
